summary: This agent skill from emilkowalski/skills distils Apple's WWDC design talks, chiefly Designing Fluid Interfaces (WWDC 2018), and translates them to the web with CSS, Pointer Events, requestAnimationFrame and spring libraries such as Motion. Its core idea is that an interface feels alive when motion starts from the current on-screen value, inherits the user's velocity, projects momentum forward and can be grabbed and reversed at any moment, with springs as the tool that makes this natural. It gives exact values: Apple's spring damping and response pairs, a momentum projection function, a rubber-band formula, ~10px gesture hysteresis, press feedback at scale(0.97) over 100ms, and type tracking of -0.02em for display text. It also covers translucent materials and depth, audio-haptic feedback, three accessibility media queries (reduced motion, reduced transparency, more contrast), size-specific typography, Apple's eight design principles and a short design process. For a design system it is a ready set of motion, material, typography and interaction standards that can be written as tokens and component rules.
key_ideas: Fluid means motion starts from the current on-screen value, inherits the user's velocity, projects momentum and can be grabbed and reversed at any instant.
Response is the foundation: give feedback on pointer-down and remove every non-essential delay on the input path.
Direct manipulation means 1:1 tracking that respects where the user grabbed the element.
Interruptibility is the single most important principle; never lock out input and always animate from the live presentation value.
Use springs for anything a user can touch, described by damping ratio and response rather than mass, stiffness and damping.
Critically damped springs (damping 1.0) are the default; bounce (damping ~0.8) is reserved for interactions that carried momentum.
Hand the release velocity to the spring and project the resting point from velocity before choosing a snap target.
Keep spatial consistency: enter and exit along the same path, and anchor popovers and sheets to their trigger.
Rubber-band at boundaries instead of stopping hard.
Translucent materials express hierarchy; heavier materials for structure, lighter for interactive elements, and never light glass on light glass.
Sound, haptics and visuals must be causal, fire on the same frame, and be used only where they earn their place.
Reduced motion means a gentler, non-vestibular equivalent (cross-fades), not no feedback; also honour reduced transparency and more contrast.
Typography changes with size: size-specific tracking, leading inverse to size, hierarchy from weight, size and leading together, and respect for the user's text size.
Apple's eight principles (purpose, agency, responsibility, familiarity, flexibility, simplicity, craft, delight) are the names to reason with.
Prototype interactively, design interaction and visuals together, and review motion frame by frame.

entities.name: Motion / Framer Motion
entities.description: Spring animation library whose bounce and duration API maps closely to Apple's damping and response, and which takes absolute px/s velocity.

entities.name: Pointer Events
entities.description: Web input API used with setPointerCapture for 1:1 drag tracking.

entities.name: requestAnimationFrame
entities.description: The web's display-synced clock, the counterpart of Apple's CADisplayLink.

entities.name: CADisplayLink
entities.description: Apple's display-synced timer, named as the native equivalent of requestAnimationFrame.

entities.name: backdrop-filter
entities.description: CSS property used to approximate Apple's translucent materials on the web.

entities.name: Vibration API
entities.description: Web API for haptics that must fire on the same frame as the visual change.

entities.name: Vaul
entities.description: Bottom-sheet library named as an example of momentum projection done well.

entities.name: Embla
entities.description: Carousel library named as an example of momentum projection done well.

entities.name: Control Center
entities.description: iOS feature whose modules grow up and out toward the finger, the example of hinting in the direction of a gesture.

entities.name: Dynamic Type
entities.description: Apple's user text-size setting; the skill says layouts should scale with it.

entities.name: Damping ratio
entities.description: Spring parameter that controls overshoot; 1.0 is critically damped, below 1.0 bounces.

entities.name: Response
entities.description: Spring parameter in seconds for how quickly the value reaches the target; not a duration.

entities.name: Presentation value
entities.description: The live on-screen value an interrupted animation must start from.

entities.name: Additive animations
entities.description: iOS's native way of carrying velocity through a re-targeted animation.

entities.name: Momentum projection
entities.description: Using release velocity to predict where a flicked element would come to rest, then snapping near that point.

entities.name: Rubber-banding
entities.description: Progressive resistance past a boundary instead of a hard stop.

entities.name: Hysteresis
entities.description: A small movement threshold or hit padding (~10px) before a gesture commits or a tap cancels.

entities.name: Vibrancy
entities.description: Keeping text legible over translucent surfaces with higher contrast, heavier weight and slightly wider letter-spacing.

entities.name: Scroll edge effect
entities.description: A small blur or gradient mask where content meets floating chrome, used instead of a hard divider.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Motion should start from the current value, inherit velocity, project momentum and be interruptible; enter and exit along the same path; hint toward the outcome; motion is designed together with visuals.

topics.name: Spring animation
topics.summary: Use springs for anything touchable, described by damping ratio and response; damping 1.0 by default, ~0.8 only after momentum; Apple's values for move (1.0/0.4), rotation (0.8/0.4) and drawer (0.8/0.3); Motion mapping bounce 0 or 0.2 with duration 0.4.

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Press feedback transitions transform over 100ms ease-out; reversible transitions mirror their easing with inverse cubic-bezier control points; a spring's response is not a duration.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: 1:1 tracking with pointer capture and grab offset, velocity history, velocity handoff, momentum projection with deceleration rate 0.998 or 0.99, rubber-banding with constant 0.55, ~10px hysteresis, parallel gesture detection and commit-or-reverse by velocity sign.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Buttons highlight instantly on press with scale(0.97); taps commit on release and can be cancelled by dragging away; feedback is continuous during a gesture.

topics.name: Animation performance
topics.summary: Animate only transform and opacity, use requestAnimationFrame, hint with will-change, keep per-frame change below the perception threshold, and use subtle motion blur or stretch for very fast motion.

topics.name: Reduced motion
topics.summary: Reduced motion swaps slides, springs and parallax for short opacity cross-fades and drops overshoot while keeping helpful opacity and colour changes; also avoid full-viewport moving backgrounds, ~0.2 Hz loops and abrupt brightness jumps.

topics.name: Accessibility
topics.summary: Components respond to prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-reduced-transparency and prefers-contrast: more, respect the user's text size with rem/em spacing, and keep text legible over translucent surfaces.

topics.name: Depth, shadows and borders
topics.summary: Translucent materials convey hierarchy; bigger surfaces get stronger blur and deeper shadow; context-aware shadows; scrims for modal tasks only; scroll edge effects instead of 1px dividers; a bright top border as light catching the material.

topics.name: Typography
topics.summary: Tracking is size-specific (negative for display, e.g. -0.02em; near 0 for body); leading tightens as size grows (1.05 display, 1.5 body); hierarchy from weight, size and leading together; system font by default; font-optical-sizing: auto.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Build hierarchy with order, spacing and contrast so the most important thing is the most obvious, and in type with weight, size and leading as a set.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Proximity implies relationship; place controls near what they affect and mirror what they change; use rem/em spacing so layouts grow with text size.

topics.name: Drawers and sheets
topics.summary: Sheets use a spring of damping 0.8 and response 0.3; flicks project to a snap point; a grabbed closing sheet follows the finger; stacked sheets progressively dim and push back their parents.

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Popovers and menus originate from their trigger via transform-origin; modal tasks pair the surface with a dimming scrim while non-blocking panels use translucency without a scrim; confirmation dialogs are only for destructive, irreversible actions.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Buttons respond on pointer-down with an instant scale(0.97) press state and commit on release, with ~10px hit padding.

topics.name: Feedback, empty and loading states
topics.summary: Feedback comes in four kinds (status, completion, warning, error); confirm meaningful actions, expose ongoing status, warn before problems; sound and haptics only for meaningful moments.

topics.name: Forms and inputs
topics.summary: Validate inline rather than on submit.

topics.name: Navigation and sidebars
topics.summary: Every screen answers where am I, where can I go, what's there and how do I get out; nav items get specific names like Progress or Library rather than Home; sidebars use heavier materials.

topics.name: Content and microcopy
topics.summary: Plain language without jargon, fewer steps, and direct, specific labels over safe generic ones.

topics.name: Dark mode and themes
topics.summary: Colours should adapt to light and dark, and theme changes between dark and light should be eased to avoid abrupt brightness jumps.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Apple's eight principles; craft means every spacing, timing and alignment value is a deliberate, defensible choice; delight comes from getting the other seven right.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Prototype interactively, design interaction and visuals together, test with real people in real context and review motion in slow motion.

topics.name: Prototyping
topics.summary: An interactive demo is worth a million static designs and sets a concrete bar that prevents a mediocre final build.

topics.name: Web implementation (CSS and React)
topics.summary: Code for press feedback, pointer capture with grab offset, Motion springs, projection and rubber-band functions, a backdrop-filter toolbar, reduced-motion and reduced-transparency media queries, and a display type style.

claims.claim: An interface feels alive when motion starts from the current on-screen value, inherits the user's velocity, projects momentum forward and can be grabbed and reversed at any instant.
Springs make fluid motion natural because they are inherently interruptible and velocity-aware.
Apple frames design as serving four human needs: safety/predictability, understanding, achievement and joy.
The moment lag appears, the feeling of directness falls off a cliff.
Waiting for click or touch-up to show feedback feels dead.
claims.evidence: Respond on pointer-down, not on release

claims.claim: Snapping a dragged element to its center on grab breaks the illusion immediately.
Starting an interrupted animation from the logical or target value causes a visible jump.
claims.evidence: Always animate from the presentation (current) value

claims.claim: CSS transitions and @keyframes cannot be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight, while springs animate from the current value by default.
claims.evidence: Avoid CSS transitions and @keyframes for anything gesture-driven

claims.claim: Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a brick wall.
claims.evidence: When a gesture reverses, blend velocity

claims.claim: A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.
claims.evidence: Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs

claims.claim: A pre-scripted fixed-duration animation cannot respond to new input; a spring can, because new input just changes the target.
Apple deliberately replaced mass, stiffness and damping with two designer-friendly parameters, damping ratio and response.
claims.evidence: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet

claims.claim: A spring has no fixed duration; its settle time emerges from its parameters.
Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right.
claims.evidence: Add bounce (damping ~0.8) only when the gesture itself carried momentum

claims.claim: Apple ships damping 1.0 / response 0.4 for move or reposition (e.g. PiP), 0.8 / 0.4 for rotation and 0.8 / 0.3 for drawer or sheet.
Motion's bounce and duration spring API maps closely to Apple's damping and response.
Continuing the animation at the finger's exact velocity after release is the detail that most separates fluid from fine.
Framer Motion and Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly through the velocity option.
claims.evidence: Framer Motion / Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly

claims.claim: Projecting the resting position from velocity is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element.
Apple ships an exponential-decay projection, not the textbook v²/(2·decel).
Momentum projection is standard behaviour in good bottom-sheets and carousels such as Vaul and Embla.
claims.evidence: This is the standard behavior in good bottom-sheets and carousels

claims.claim: Entering from the right and exiting out the bottom feels disconnected and confusing.
claims.evidence: Enter and exit along the same path

claims.claim: Humans predict a final state from a trajectory.
claims.evidence: 8. Hint in the direction of the gesture

claims.claim: A hard stop at an edge reads as frozen, while continuous resistance reads as responsive but with nothing more there.
Recognizers that only report a final state throw away the continuous tracking needed for feedback.
claims.evidence: Detect all plausible gestures in parallel

claims.claim: Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps.
Smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.
For very fast motion, a subtle motion blur or stretch encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak.
Stacking a light translucent surface on another makes legibility collapse.
claims.evidence: Never stack a light translucent surface on another

claims.claim: Over-feedback trains users to ignore all feedback.
Latency between visual, sound and haptic destroys the illusion.
Large display text reads with letters too far apart as it grows, so it wants negative tracking; small text wants slightly positive tracking.
Weight adds presence without taking more space.
The platform system font already ships optical sizing, tracking tables and legibility tuning.
claims.evidence: Default to the platform's system font

claims.claim: Overusing confirmation dialogs trains people to click through.
Burying everything in one place looks minimal but isn't simple.
Jittery scroll, misaligned icons and layouts that break on rotation read as carelessness.
If you need a label to explain a control, the mapping is weak.
Specific labels create predictability.
claims.evidence: Direct, specific labels beat safe generic ones

claims.claim: A working prototype sets a concrete bar that prevents a mediocre final implementation.
An interface is fluid when it behaves like the physical world: things respond instantly, move continuously, carry momentum, resist at boundaries and can be redirected mid-motion.

quotes: Touch and content should move together.
The thought and the gesture happen in parallel.
If something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came.

rules.rule: Respond on pointer-down, not on release: highlight a button the instant it is pressed.
rules.why: Waiting for click or touch-up to show feedback feels dead; response is the foundation everything else is built on.
rules.evidence: Respond on pointer-down, not on release

rules.rule: Give buttons an instant press state: on :active apply transform: scale(0.97) with transition: transform 100ms ease-out.
rules.why: Feedback lives on the press, and it's instant.
rules.evidence: Feedback lives on the press, and it's instant

rules.rule: Audit every latency on the input path (debounces, artificial timers, transition waits, the ~300ms tap delay) and remove anything that is not essential.
rules.why: The moment lag appears, the feeling of directness falls off a cliff; anything non-essential on the input path is a regression.
rules.evidence: Be vigilant about every latency

rules.rule: For a drag, slider or drawer, update the UI 1:1 with the pointer the whole way through the interaction; never animate only when the gesture completes.
rules.why: Feedback must be continuous during the interaction, not just at the end.
rules.evidence: update the UI 1:1 with the pointer the whole way through

rules.rule: Keep a dragged element glued to the finger and preserve the offset from where the user grabbed it; do not snap the element's center to the pointer on grab.
rules.why: Touch and content should move together; snapping to the center breaks the illusion immediately.
rules.evidence: 2. Direct manipulation — 1:1 tracking

rules.rule: Track drags with Pointer Events and call setPointerCapture on pointerdown.
rules.why: Tracking then continues even when the pointer leaves the element's bounds.
rules.evidence: so tracking continues even when the pointer leaves the element's bounds

rules.rule: Record a short position and timestamp history (the last few pointermove events), not just the current point.
rules.why: You will need velocity at release.
rules.evidence: not just the current point — you'll need velocity at release

rules.rule: Make every animation interruptible and redirectable at any moment, so a user can grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it without waiting.
rules.why: Interruptibility is the single most important principle; the thought and the gesture happen in parallel.
rules.evidence: 3. Interruptibility — the single most important principle

rules.rule: When a user grabs a closing modal or sheet again, make it follow the finger immediately rather than finishing the close and then reopening.
rules.why: Every animation must be interruptible and redirectable at any moment.
rules.evidence: A closing modal the user grabs again should follow the finger

rules.rule: Never lock out input during a transition.
rules.why: Users must be able to redirect motion at any instant.
rules.evidence: Never lock out input during a transition

rules.rule: On interrupt, read the element's live on-screen (presentation) transform and start the new animation from there, never from the target or logical value.
rules.why: Starting from the logical or target value causes a visible jump.
rules.evidence: read the element's live on-screen transform and start the new animation from there

rules.rule: Do not use CSS transitions or @keyframes for anything gesture-driven; use springs.
rules.why: They cannot be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight, while springs animate from the current value by default.
rules.evidence: they can't be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight

rules.rule: When a gesture reverses, blend velocity through the re-target instead of hard-cutting to a new animation; choose a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity.
rules.why: Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a brick wall (iOS does this natively with additive animations).
rules.evidence: When a gesture reverses, blend velocity — don't hard-cut it

rules.rule: Animate 2D motion with two independent springs, one for X and one for Y, not one spring on the 2D distance.
rules.why: A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.
rules.evidence: Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs

rules.rule: Use springs, not pre-scripted fixed-duration animations, for anything a user can touch.
rules.why: A fixed-duration animation cannot respond to new input; with a spring, new input just changes the target and motion stays continuous.
rules.evidence: 4. Behavior over animation — use springs

rules.rule: Specify springs with two parameters, damping ratio and response, rather than mass, stiffness and damping.
rules.why: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet with these two designer-friendly parameters.
rules.evidence: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet

rules.rule: Do not treat a spring's response as a duration; its settle time emerges from the parameters.
rules.why: A spring has no fixed duration; response is how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds.
rules.evidence: This is not "duration"

rules.rule: Default UI springs to damping 1.0 (critically damped, no overshoot) with response 0.3-0.4.
rules.why: Critically damped motion is graceful and non-distracting; the source calls damping 1.0 everywhere by default a safe house style.
rules.evidence: (critically damped) — graceful and non-distracting

rules.rule: Add bounce (damping ~0.8, response 0.3-0.4) only when the gesture itself carried momentum, such as a flick, a throw or a drag release.
rules.why: Overshoot on a card you flicked feels right.
rules.evidence: only when the gesture itself carried momentum

rules.rule: Do not overshoot on elements that appear without a gesture, such as a menu that just faded in.
rules.why: Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong.
rules.evidence: Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong

rules.rule: For moving or repositioning an element (e.g. picture-in-picture), use a spring with damping 1.0 and response 0.4.
rules.why: These are the values Apple ships for move/reposition.
rules.evidence: Move / reposition (e.g. PiP)

rules.rule: For rotation, use a spring with damping 0.8 and response 0.4.
rules.why: These are the values Apple ships for rotation.
rules.evidence: Rotation | `0.8` | `0.4`

rules.rule: For drawers and sheets, use a spring with damping 0.8 and response 0.3.
rules.why: These are the values Apple ships for drawer/sheet.
rules.evidence: Drawer / sheet | `0.8` | `0.3`

rules.rule: In Motion / Framer Motion, express the default spring as { type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 } and a momentum spring as { type: 'spring', bounce: 0.2, duration: 0.4 }.
rules.why: Motion's bounce + duration API maps closely to Apple's damping + response; bounce is reserved for momentum-driven, physical interactions.
rules.evidence: Web mapping (Motion / Framer Motion)

rules.rule: When a gesture ends, pass the pointer's release velocity as the spring's initial velocity so the animation continues at the finger's exact speed.
rules.why: There is then no visible seam between dragging and animating; this detail most separates fluid from fine.
rules.evidence: 5. Velocity handoff — the seam between drag and animation

rules.rule: If the spring API wants relative velocity, normalise the release velocity by the remaining distance: relativeVelocity = gestureVelocity / (targetValue − currentValue).
rules.why: Some spring APIs take relative velocity; e.g. at y=50 with target y=150 and the finger moving 50px/s, the initial velocity is 50 / 100 = 0.5.
rules.evidence: normalize it by the remaining distance to the target

rules.rule: In Motion / Framer Motion, hand the raw absolute px/s release velocity to the velocity option instead of normalising it.
rules.why: Framer Motion / Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly.
rules.evidence: Framer Motion / Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly

rules.rule: Do not snap to the boundary nearest the release point; project the resting position from the release velocity and snap to the target nearest that projected point.
rules.why: This is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element, like scroll deceleration.
rules.evidence: 6. Momentum projection — animate to where the gesture is going

rules.rule: Project momentum with Apple's exponential-decay function: (initialVelocity / 1000) * decelerationRate / (1 - decelerationRate), with decelerationRate ≈ 0.998 for normal scroll feel or 0.99 for snappier, then add it to the current position.
rules.why: It is Apple's exact projection function from the Designing Fluid Interfaces sample code.
rules.evidence: Apple's exact projection function

rules.rule: Do not use the physics-textbook projection v²/(2·decel).
rules.why: It is not what Apple ships; use the exponential-decay form.
rules.evidence: use the exponential-decay form above

rules.rule: Decide whether to reverse or commit a gesture at release by the sign of the velocity, not by the position.
rules.why: Listed in the Quick Reference as the way to decide reverse vs. commit.
rules.evidence: Decide reverse vs. commit

rules.rule: Make elements enter and exit along the same path: a panel that slides in from the right must dismiss to the right.
rules.why: In-from-right / out-the-bottom feels disconnected and confusing; if something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came.
rules.evidence: Enter and exit along the same path

rules.rule: Make menus, popovers and sheets originate from the element that triggered them by setting transform-origin to the trigger, so popovers scale from their trigger, not their center.
rules.why: The spatial relationship between button and content becomes obvious.
rules.evidence: Anchor interactions to their source

rules.rule: Mirror the easing on reversible transitions using inverse cubic-bézier control points for the two directions.
rules.why: The outbound path then matches the return path.
rules.evidence: Mirror the easing on reversible transitions

rules.rule: Make intermediate frames telegraph where the motion is going, e.g. growing up and out toward the finger, rather than interpolating blindly.
rules.why: Humans predict a final state from a trajectory, as with Control Center modules.
rules.evidence: 8. Hint in the direction of the gesture

rules.rule: At a boundary, rubber-band with progressively increasing resistance instead of stopping hard.
rules.why: A hard stop reads as frozen; continuous resistance reads as responsive but with nothing more there.
rules.evidence: 9. Rubber-banding — soft boundaries

rules.rule: Compute rubber-band displacement as (overshoot * dimension * constant) / (dimension + constant * Math.abs(overshoot)) with constant = 0.55.
rules.why: The further past the bound, the less the element follows; real things slow before they stop.
rules.evidence: function rubberband

rules.rule: For taps, highlight on touch-down and commit on touch-up.
rules.why: Feedback is instant on press while the action waits for release.
rules.evidence: highlight on touch-*down* (instant), commit on touch-*up*

rules.rule: Add ~10px of hysteresis or hit padding around tap targets, and let users cancel a tap by dragging away and back.
rules.why: Part of the tap feel checklist.
rules.evidence: Add ~10px of hysteresis/hit padding

rules.rule: For drags and swipes, require a small movement threshold (~10px) before committing to a direction, then track 1:1.
rules.why: Part of the drag/swipe feel checklist.
rules.evidence: require a small movement threshold (hysteresis, ~10px) before committing to a direction

rules.rule: Detect all plausible gestures in parallel from the first move, then confidently cancel the losers once intent is clear.
rules.why: Recognizers that only report a final state throw away the continuous tracking needed for feedback.
rules.evidence: Detect all plausible gestures in parallel from the first move

rules.rule: Do not use gesture recognizers that only report a final state (swipeleft-type events).
rules.why: They throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.
rules.evidence: Avoid recognizers that only report a final state

rules.rule: Only add double-tap detection where a double-tap action truly exists.
rules.why: Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps.
rules.evidence: Minimize disambiguation delays

rules.rule: Keep the per-frame positional change below the perception threshold.
rules.why: It avoids strobing; smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just frame rate.
rules.evidence: 11. Frame-level smoothness

rules.rule: For very fast motion, add a subtle motion blur or stretch.
rules.why: It encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak.
rules.evidence: encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak

rules.rule: Drive frame-by-frame animation with requestAnimationFrame.
rules.why: It is the web's display-synced clock (Apple uses CADisplayLink).
rules.evidence: is the web's display-synced clock

rules.rule: Animate only compositor-friendly properties: transform and opacity.
rules.why: Part of frame-level smoothness.
rules.evidence: Animate only compositor-friendly properties

rules.rule: Hint with will-change where motion is imminent.
rules.why: Part of frame-level smoothness.
rules.evidence: where motion is imminent

rules.rule: Build nav bars, toolbars and sheets as translucent layers (backdrop-filter: blur() plus a semi-transparent background) with content scrolling underneath, not opaque bars that consume a fixed strip.
rules.why: Translucent materials act as a floating functional layer that brings structure without stealing focus.
rules.evidence: Build nav/toolbars/sheets as translucent layers

rules.rule: Use darker, heavier materials to separate structural regions such as sidebars, and lighter materials to draw attention to interactive elements such as buttons.
rules.why: Material weight encodes hierarchy.
rules.evidence: Material weight encodes hierarchy

rules.rule: Never stack a light translucent surface on another.
rules.why: Legibility collapses.
rules.evidence: Never stack a light translucent surface on another

rules.rule: Make bigger surfaces read as thicker: give them stronger blur and a deeper shadow than small chips.
rules.why: Bigger surfaces should read as thicker material.
rules.evidence: Bigger surfaces should read as thicker

rules.rule: Use context-aware shadow: heavier over busy or text content for separation, lighter over plain backgrounds.
rules.why: A heavier shadow over busy or text content gives separation.
rules.evidence: Consider context-aware shadow

rules.rule: For a modal task, pair the surface with a dimming scrim and push the background back or down.
rules.why: Dim to focus.
rules.evidence: Dim to focus, separate to keep flow

rules.rule: For a parallel, non-blocking panel, use translucency and offset without a scrim.
rules.why: Separate to keep flow, so the flow is not broken.
rules.evidence: A parallel, non-blocking panel uses translucency and offset without a scrim

rules.rule: For stacked sheets, progressively dim and push back each parent layer.
rules.why: Part of dimming to focus.
rules.evidence: For stacked sheets, progressively dim and push back each parent layer

rules.rule: Over blurred or translucent surfaces, do not use flat gray text; use higher contrast, a slightly heavier weight and a small letter-spacing bump.
rules.why: Vibrancy keeps text legible over changing backgrounds.
rules.evidence: Vibrancy keeps text legible over changing backgrounds

rules.rule: Put color on a solid layer, not on the translucent foreground.
rules.why: Part of keeping content legible over translucent materials.
rules.evidence: Put color on a solid layer, not the translucent foreground

rules.rule: Instead of a 1px border under a sticky header, fade a small blur or gradient mask where content meets floating chrome, and only where floating UI actually overlaps content.
rules.why: Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers.
rules.evidence: Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers

rules.rule: For glass or blur surfaces, animate blur radius and scale together on enter and exit rather than a plain opacity fade.
rules.why: The surface reads as a real material arriving.
rules.evidence: Materialize, don't just fade

rules.rule: Style a light translucent toolbar as background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6); backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%); border-top: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.4).
rules.why: The bright top edge reads as light catching the material.
rules.evidence: bright top edge = light catching the material

rules.rule: Trigger multimodal feedback on the actual causal event (the toggle flipping, the item snapping home) and match its character to the physicality of the action.
rules.why: Causality: it must be obvious what caused the feedback.
rules.evidence: it must be obvious what caused the feedback

rules.rule: Fire the visual, the sound and the haptic on the same frame; do not let a CSS transition lag the audio or Vibration API haptic.
rules.why: Harmony: latency between them destroys the illusion.
rules.evidence: Latency between them destroys the illusion

rules.rule: Reserve haptics and sound for meaningful moments (success, error, commit, snap).
rules.why: Utility: over-feedback trains users to ignore all of it.
rules.evidence: add feedback only where it earns its place

rules.rule: Treat reduced motion as a gentler, non-vestibular equivalent, not as removing feedback.
rules.why: Reduced motion doesn't mean no feedback.
rules.evidence: 14. Reduced motion & accessibility

rules.rule: Respond to three independent signals and bake them into your components: prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-reduced-transparency and prefers-contrast.
rules.why: Reduced motion doesn't mean no feedback; it means a gentler, non-vestibular equivalent, and each signal needs its own treatment.
rules.evidence: Respond to three independent signals

rules.rule: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, replace slides, springs and parallax with short opacity cross-fades or static transitions, drop elastic and overshoot, and keep opacity and colour changes that aid comprehension.
rules.why: It gives a gentler, non-vestibular equivalent.
rules.evidence: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce

rules.rule: Under prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce, make translucent surfaces frostier or solid: raise background opacity and drop the blur.
rules.why: It is one of the three independent signals the source says to bake into components.
rules.evidence: prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce

rules.rule: Under prefers-contrast: more, use near-solid backgrounds with a defined, contrasting border.
rules.why: It is one of the three independent signals the source says to bake into components.
rules.evidence: prefers-contrast: more

rules.rule: Avoid full-viewport moving backgrounds.
rules.why: Listed among motion to avoid for accessibility.
rules.evidence: avoid full-viewport moving backgrounds

rules.rule: Avoid slow looping oscillations near 0.2 Hz (one cycle per 5s).
rules.why: Listed among motion to avoid for accessibility.
rules.evidence: slow looping oscillations (near 0.2 Hz / one cycle per 5s)

rules.rule: Avoid abrupt brightness jumps; ease theme changes between dark and light.
rules.why: Listed among changes to avoid for accessibility.
rules.evidence: abrupt brightness jumps (ease dark↔light theme changes)

rules.rule: Make large moving objects semi-transparent while they travel.
rules.why: Part of the reduced-motion and accessibility guidance.
rules.evidence: Make large moving objects semi-transparent while they travel

rules.rule: During a large reposition, fade big surfaces out and fade them back in once settled.
rules.why: Part of the reduced-motion and accessibility guidance.
rules.evidence: fade big surfaces out during a large reposition

rules.rule: Make tracking (letter-spacing) size-specific; never use one letter-spacing value for all sizes.
rules.why: A fixed letter-spacing is wrong somewhere.
rules.evidence: Tracking (letter-spacing) is size-specific — never one value for all sizes

rules.rule: Give large display text negative tracking (e.g. letter-spacing: -0.02em) and small text slightly positive tracking; leave body text near 0.
rules.why: Letters read too far apart as text grows; small text needs slightly positive tracking for legibility.
rules.evidence: letters read too far apart as they grow

rules.rule: Set leading (line-height) inversely to size: tight on large headings (e.g. 1.05 for display), looser on body copy (e.g. 1.5).
rules.why: Leading tracks size inversely.
rules.evidence: Leading (line-height) tracks size inversely

rules.rule: Increase line-height for scripts with tall ascenders and descenders.
rules.why: Part of the leading guidance.
rules.evidence: Increase it for scripts with tall ascenders/descenders

rules.rule: Tighten line-height for dense, information-heavy UI.
rules.why: Part of the leading guidance.
rules.evidence: tighten it for dense, information-heavy UI

rules.rule: Build type hierarchy from weight, size and leading as a set, not from size alone, and emphasise with weight.
rules.why: Weight adds presence without taking more space.
rules.evidence: Build hierarchy from weight + size + leading as a set

rules.rule: Respect the user's text-size setting (Dynamic Type): scale layout with the text by using rem/em for spacing, not fixed px.
rules.why: A larger font then does not break the layout.
rules.evidence: Respect the user's text-size setting (Dynamic Type)

rules.rule: Default to the platform's system font (e.g. font: 100%/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif) before a custom face; override only with a reason.
rules.why: The system font already ships optical sizing, tracking tables and legibility tuning.
rules.evidence: Default to the platform's system font

rules.rule: Style display text with fluid size, tight leading, negative tracking and optical sizing, e.g. font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.02em; font-optical-sizing: auto.
rules.why: Apple designs type to change shape with size; the same discipline applies on the web.
rules.evidence: font-optical-sizing: auto

rules.rule: Decide what not to build; spend the user's time, attention and trust only on features that pay off.
rules.why: Purpose: every feature asks for the user's time, attention and trust.
rules.evidence: Every feature asks for the user's time, attention, and trust

rules.rule: Keep people in control by offering choices instead of forcing a single path.
rules.why: Agency.
rules.evidence: Keep people in control: offer choices, don't force a single path

rules.rule: Provide easy undo for slips, and use a confirmation dialog only for genuinely destructive, irreversible actions, sparingly.
rules.why: Forgiveness backs agency; overusing confirmations trains people to click through.
rules.evidence: easy undo for slips, a confirmation dialog only for genuinely destructive, irreversible actions

rules.rule: Ask for private data at the right moment, only for what is needed, and transparently.
rules.why: Responsibility: act in the user's interest.
rules.evidence: Privacy: ask at the right moment, only for what's needed, transparently

rules.rule: Anticipate misuse and harm, especially with AI features: add previews, confirmations and disclaimers, and cut a feature whose risk outweighs its value.
rules.why: Responsibility: e.g. an allergy-aware recipe app must not suggest a harmful ingredient.
rules.evidence: Safety: anticipate misuse and harm

rules.rule: Use metaphors that are neither too literal nor too abstract (a trash can means delete) and honour their physics.
rules.why: Familiarity: build on what people already know.
rules.evidence: Use metaphors that are neither too literal nor too abstract

rules.rule: Keep things that look the same behaving the same and living in the same place (e.g. close is always top-left on macOS).
rules.why: People can then predict what happens next.
rules.evidence: Be consistent: things that look the same must behave the same

rules.rule: Only break a familiar pattern if you can prove the new one is better, and test it rather than assume.
rules.why: Familiarity.
rules.evidence: Only break a familiar pattern if you can prove it's better

rules.rule: Adapt to the platform and situation: quick touch on iPhone, deep workflows with precise pointer control on desktop.
rules.why: Flexibility: design for different contexts, devices and abilities.
rules.evidence: desktop = deep workflows with precise pointer control

rules.rule: Design inclusively for age, language, expertise and accessibility.
rules.why: Flexibility: the full range of abilities.
rules.evidence: Design inclusively (age, language, expertise, accessibility)

rules.rule: When no single layout fits everyone, let people personalise: rearrange controls and hide what they do not use.
rules.why: Flexibility.
rules.evidence: let people personalize

rules.rule: Do not bury everything in one place to look minimal; strip the unnecessary so the core purpose shines.
rules.why: Simplicity is not minimalism; burying everything looks minimal but isn't simple.
rules.evidence: Simplicity — not minimalism

rules.rule: Be concise: plain language, no jargon, fewer steps.
rules.why: Simplicity.
rules.evidence: Be concise (plain language, no jargon, fewer steps)

rules.rule: Use hierarchy (order, spacing, contrast) so the most important thing is the most obvious.
rules.why: Simplicity: be clear.
rules.evidence: clear (use hierarchy — order, spacing, contrast)

rules.rule: Make every element earn its place, and add context where it simplifies (e.g. a video scrubber that shows time remaining).
rules.why: Sometimes adding context simplifies.
rules.evidence: Every element earns its place

rules.rule: Show the common path first and put advanced options one level deeper.
rules.why: Simplicity.
rules.evidence: Show the common path first, advanced options one level deeper

rules.rule: Make every spacing, timing and alignment value a deliberate choice you can defend; nothing is random.
rules.why: Craft: uncompromising attention to detail builds trust.
rules.evidence: Nothing is random

rules.rule: Use colours that adapt to light and dark, clear iconography and responsive animations that give immediate, natural feedback.
rules.why: Craft: uncompromising attention to detail builds trust.
rules.evidence: colors that adapt to light/dark, clear iconography

rules.rule: Do not ship jittery scroll, misaligned icons or layouts that break on rotation.
rules.why: They read as carelessness.
rules.evidence: Jittery scroll, misaligned icons, and layouts that break on rotation read as carelessness

rules.rule: Keep evolving the design as features and hardware change.
rules.why: Craft needs iteration and longevity.
rules.evidence: Craft needs iteration and longevity

rules.rule: Decide the emotion you want people to feel (calm, confident, excited) and reinforce it in every decision, instead of tacking delight on top.
rules.why: Delight is the result of getting the other seven principles right, not confetti.
rules.evidence: Decide the emotion you want people to feel

rules.rule: Cover the four kinds of feedback (status, completion, warning, error): confirm meaningful actions, expose ongoing status and warn before problems.
rules.why: Feedback comes in four kinds: status, completion, warning, error.
rules.evidence: Feedback comes in four kinds

rules.rule: Validate form input inline, not on submit.
rules.why: Listed as a tactical feedback rule.
rules.evidence: validate inline (not on submit)

rules.rule: Make every screen answer: Where am I? Where can I go? What's there? How do I get out? Never trap the user.
rules.why: Wayfinding.
rules.evidence: Every screen should answer: Where am I?

rules.rule: Place a control near what it affects and arrange controls to mirror what they change.
rules.why: Proximity implies relationship; if you need a label to explain a control, the mapping is weak.
rules.evidence: Grouping & mapping

rules.rule: Name navigation items for their contents (e.g. "Progress", "Library"), not with vague umbrellas like "Home".
rules.why: Direct, specific labels create predictability.
rules.evidence: Direct, specific labels beat safe generic ones

rules.rule: Prototype interactively rather than relying on static designs.
rules.why: You discover the interface by building and playing with it, and a working prototype sets a concrete bar that prevents a mediocre final implementation.
rules.evidence: Prototype interactively

rules.rule: Design interaction and visuals together; do not add motion as a layer after the pixels.
rules.why: You shouldn't be able to tell where one ends and the other begins.
rules.evidence: Design interaction and visuals together

rules.rule: Test with real people in real context.
rules.why: Part of the process guidance.
rules.evidence: Test with real people in real context

rules.rule: Review motion with fresh eyes by playing it in slow motion or frame by frame.
rules.why: It catches what is invisible at full speed.
rules.evidence: play it in slow motion / frame-by-frame

rules.rule: Reason with Apple's eight principles by name (purpose, agency, responsibility, familiarity, flexibility, simplicity, craft, delight) when making and defending design decisions.
rules.why: The motion and craft guidance serves these eight principles; the source says to use them as the names you reason with.
rules.evidence: Use these as the names you reason with

decisions.question: Should touchable UI animate with fixed-duration transitions or with springs?

options.name: Fixed-duration animations (CSS transitions, @keyframes)
options.effect: Pre-scripted motion that cannot respond to new input or be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight.
options.when: The source does not recommend it for anything gesture-driven.

options.name: Springs
options.effect: New input just changes the target and motion stays continuous; they animate from the current value and carry velocity.

decisions.recommendation: Springs for anything a user can touch, because they are interruptible and velocity-aware.

decisions.question: How should spring settings be expressed?

options.name: Mass, stiffness and damping
options.effect: The physics triplet that Apple deliberately replaced.

options.name: Damping ratio and response
options.effect: Damping controls overshoot (1.0 no bounce, lower bouncier); response in seconds controls snappiness; settle time emerges rather than being a set duration.
options.when: Default; on the web, Motion's bounce + duration maps closely.

decisions.recommendation: Think in damping ratio and response, designer-friendly parameters Apple adopted.
decisions.evidence: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet

decisions.question: How much bounce should springs have?

options.name: Critically damped (damping 1.0, bounce 0)
options.effect: Smooth settle with no overshoot; graceful and non-distracting.

options.name: Under-damped (damping ~0.8, bounce 0.2)
options.effect: Slight overshoot that feels like physical momentum.
options.when: Only after a gesture that carried momentum: a flick, throw or drag release.

decisions.recommendation: damping 1.0 everywhere by default; reserve bounce for momentum-driven, physical interactions.

decisions.question: Where should a flicked element land on release?

options.name: Nearest boundary from the release point
options.effect: Ignores the flick's speed, so a throw does not feel like a throw.

options.name: Nearest snap point to the momentum-projected endpoint
options.effect: Uses velocity to predict the resting point like scroll deceleration, so a flick throws the element.
options.when: Bottom sheets and carousels (the source names Vaul and Embla); any flickable element [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Project with Apple's exponential-decay function (decelerationRate ≈ 0.998, or 0.99 for snappier) and snap to the point nearest the projection, then hand off velocity.

decisions.question: At release, how do you decide whether a gesture commits or reverses?

options.name: By position
options.effect: Decides from where the element is at release.

options.name: By the sign of the velocity
options.effect: Decides from the direction the finger was moving at release.

decisions.evidence: Quick Reference: Decide reverse vs. commit

decisions.question: Should bars, toolbars and sheets be opaque or translucent?

options.name: Opaque bars
options.effect: Consume a fixed strip of the screen.
options.when: The source does not recommend them for chrome; also the fallback under reduced transparency.

options.name: Translucent layers (backdrop-filter blur + semi-transparent background)
options.effect: A floating functional layer with content scrolling underneath that brings structure without stealing focus.
options.when: Nav, toolbars and sheets by default.

decisions.recommendation: Translucent layers, with heavier materials for structure and lighter ones for interactive elements, never light on light.

decisions.question: Should a secondary panel dim the content behind it?

options.name: Dimming scrim and push the background back or down
options.effect: Focuses the user on a modal task.
options.when: Modal tasks; stacked sheets progressively dim and push back each parent.

options.name: Translucency and offset without a scrim
options.effect: Separates the panel while keeping the flow unbroken.

decisions.recommendation: Dim to focus, separate to keep flow.
decisions.evidence: Dim to focus, separate to keep flow

decisions.question: How should a sticky header be separated from scrolling content?

options.name: 1px border
options.effect: A hard divider line under the header.

options.name: Scroll edge effect
options.effect: A small blur or gradient mask fades where content meets floating chrome, only where it overlaps content.

decisions.recommendation: Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers.
decisions.evidence: Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers

decisions.question: When people turn on reduced motion, what should happen?

options.name: Replace with gentler equivalents
options.effect: Slides, springs and parallax become short opacity cross-fades or static transitions; overshoot is dropped; helpful opacity and colour changes stay.

options.name: Remove all feedback
options.effect: No motion or feedback at all.
options.when: The source says reduced motion does not mean no feedback.

decisions.recommendation: Replace with a gentler, non-vestibular equivalent such as a 200ms opacity cross-fade.

decisions.question: Which user settings should components respond to?

options.name: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce
options.effect: Cross-fades instead of slides and springs.

options.name: prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce
options.effect: Frostier or solid surfaces with higher background opacity and no blur.

options.name: prefers-contrast: more
options.effect: Near-solid backgrounds with a defined, contrasting border.

options.name: Text size (Dynamic Type)
options.effect: Layout scales with the text through rem/em spacing.

decisions.recommendation: All of them, baked into components.

decisions.question: Should letter spacing be one value or change with text size?

options.name: One fixed letter-spacing
options.effect: Wrong somewhere: too loose on large text or too tight on small text.

options.name: Size-specific tracking
options.effect: Negative on large display text (e.g. -0.02em), near 0 for body, slightly positive for small text.

decisions.recommendation: Size-specific tracking: tighten headings, leave body near 0.

decisions.question: Should the UI use the system font or a custom typeface?

options.name: Platform system font (system-ui)
options.effect: Ships with optical sizing, tracking tables and legibility tuning.

options.name: Custom typeface
options.effect: A brand face that needs its own tuning [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Default to the system font; override only with a reason.
decisions.evidence: Default to the platform's system font

decisions.question: Should layouts grow when people turn up their text size?

options.name: Scale layout with text (rem/em spacing)
options.effect: A larger font does not break the layout.

options.name: Fixed px spacing
options.effect: Larger text can break the layout.

decisions.recommendation: Respect the user's text-size setting and scale layout with it.
decisions.evidence: Respect the user's text-size setting (Dynamic Type)

decisions.question: How should people recover from mistakes and destructive actions?

options.name: Easy undo
options.effect: Slips can be reversed without interruption.

options.name: Confirmation dialog
options.effect: An extra step before acting; overuse trains people to click through.
options.when: Only genuinely destructive, irreversible actions, sparingly.

decisions.recommendation: Both, each in its place: undo for slips, confirmation only for destructive, irreversible actions.

decisions.question: How much sound and haptic feedback should the product use?

options.name: Feedback on many interactions
options.effect: Over-feedback trains users to ignore all of it.

options.name: Only meaningful moments
options.effect: Sound and haptics on success, error, commit and snap, fired on the same frame as the visual.

decisions.recommendation: Reserve haptics and sound for meaningful moments.

decisions.question: When should form input be validated?

options.name: Inline
options.effect: Problems are shown as people type or leave a field [inferred].

options.name: On submit
options.effect: Problems appear only after submitting.

decisions.question: How should navigation items be labelled?

options.name: Specific labels ("Progress", "Library")
options.effect: Creates predictability about what is behind each item.

options.name: Generic umbrellas ("Home")
options.effect: Safe but vague.

decisions.recommendation: Direct, specific labels beat safe generic ones.
decisions.evidence: Direct, specific labels beat safe generic ones

process.detail: Show feedback on pointer-down (e.g. scale(0.97) over 100ms ease-out), commit on release, and remove debounces, artificial timers and the ~300ms tap delay from the input path.
On pointerdown call setPointerCapture, record the grab offset, and keep a short history of positions and timestamps from pointermove.

Wait for ~10px of movement before committing to a direction, detect plausible gestures in parallel from the first move, cancel the losers once intent is clear, and only delay taps where double-tap exists.
Update the element with the pointer every frame via transform, and past a boundary apply the rubber-band formula with constant 0.55.

Compute release velocity from the history, decide commit or reverse by the velocity's sign, project the resting point with (v/1000)·d/(1−d) using d ≈ 0.998 (or 0.99), and pick the nearest snap point to that projection.

Animate to the target with a spring given the release velocity (normalised by remaining distance if the API wants relative velocity); damping 1.0 by default, ~0.8 only after momentum; use separate X and Y springs for 2D.
Never lock input; on a new grab read the live on-screen transform and re-target from there, carrying velocity through reversals.
Exit along the entry path, set transform-origin to the trigger, mirror easing for reversible transitions, and let intermediate frames point at the outcome.
Fire sound or haptics on the causal event, on the same frame as the visual, and only for success, error, commit or snap.
Add prefers-reduced-motion (cross-fades, no overshoot), prefers-reduced-transparency (solid, no blur) and prefers-contrast: more (near-solid with a contrasting border) styles to each component.
Build an interactive prototype, design interaction and visuals together, test with real people in real context, and review motion in slow motion or frame by frame.

caveats: This is an agent skill file, not an Apple document: it says it distils and translates WWDC talks for the web, so quotes and values attributed to Apple are second-hand and were not checked against the talks here.
The Initial Response section tells the agent what to say when invoked; it is skill behaviour, not design guidance, and was left out of the rules.
The Motion bounce + duration mapping is described as mapping 'closely' to Apple's damping + response, not exactly; library APIs may change between versions.
Many values are approximate in the source (~0.8 damping, ~10px hysteresis, ~300ms tap delay, near 0.2 Hz), and the code snippets use undefined helpers (nearestSnapPoint, animateSpringTo).
The source is pinned to commit 85e8e23 of emilkowalski/skills; later commits may change it.
The toolbar CSS is a light-theme sample (white at 60%); the source gives no dark-theme values.
No media list exists for this source, so no images were reviewed.
